notes:
Docket told three pages they had forgotten a property, when what they had written was a pointer.

A common and correct way to publish structured data is to define your organisation once, give it an `@id`, and reference that `@id` from everywhere else. The reference is a stub — a type and an id, no other properties — and it is exactly what several popular SEO plugins emit.

Docket has understood this since 1.3.43: a stub is resolved against the definition it points at, and only a pointer whose target the page never provides is reported. What it did not do was say so out loud in every case.

The sentence explaining that these blocks are references — the one that turns "you forgot a property" into something you can act on — was printed only when a site had *more* markup blocks than pages. That is a real pattern, but it has nothing to do with whether a block is a reference. A site carrying exactly one stub per page, which is the ordinary shape of this idiom, fell just outside it: three blocks across three pages is not more than three, so the explanation was withheld and the finding read, in full, "Organization: missing name."

We found it on a hotel group. Three city pages, each with a single `Organization` stub pointing at `#organization`, which their own homepage defines completely — name, logo, contact point and all. Docket had already worked out that these were references. It simply did not print the part that said so.

The advice was wrong in the same breath. "Add the missing properties to the Organization block" asks you to paste a name into three pointers you wrote deliberately. So when every block of a type is a pointer, Docket now tells you what actually applies: structured data is read one page at a time, so an `@id` pointing at a definition on another page resolves to nothing on this one. Define the block on each page that references it, or remove the stub — as it stands it produces neither a rich result nor an error.

Docket judges each page's markup on its own, exactly as a search engine does, so it says the target is missing *here* without claiming it is missing everywhere.

A block that genuinely is an incomplete definition — one carrying properties of its own and still missing a required one — is reported and advised exactly as before.
